- When sentiment is consistently negative or bearish (e.g., 0.00 or -0.33), model tends to overcorrect upward — reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior period), model often overshoots and fails to correct — apply downward drag or mean-reversion bias in next 5–7 days.
- In high-event periods (e.g., >15 events/30d, net supply negative), model overestimates bullishness — reduce forecast by 3–5% relative to historical mean of same event count.
- If sentiment history shows alternating bullish/bearish cycles (e.g., 0.67 → 0.00 → 1.00), model may misread momentum — adjust for sentiment lag (forecast 1–2 days behind sentiment peak).
- In low-event or neutral sentiment (e.g., 0.33/0.67), model often underestimates volatility — increase forecast variance or add 1–2% upward buffer for sudden policy or auction shocks.
- When supply net is negative and bullish sentiment is low, model tends to ignore supply constraints — reduce forecast by 5–8% to reflect supply-side pressure.
- For 30-day horizon, model often fails to capture short-term event-driven reversals — add 1–2 day lag correction if recent event is supply-heavy or bearish sentiment persists.
